newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-GRAF HALTS HINGIS TO REACH U.S. OPEN FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF HALTS HINGIS TO REACH U.S. OPEN FINAL.

text.p: Fifteen-year-old Martina Hingis has been hailed as a future number one, but the present still belongs to Steffi Graf after her 7-5 6-3 U.S. Open semifinal victory over the teenager on Saturday.

Defending champion Graf, a four-time Open winner, will play her 29th Grand Slam final on Sunday and eighth at Flushing Meadow when she takes on twice Open champion Monica Seles in a re-match of last year's final.
The second-seeded Seles took care of fourth-seeded Spaniard Conchita Martinez in straight sets on Friday.
Graf may also have won in straight sets, but Hingis kept the pressure on the top seed in a way that belied her youth and relative big-match inexperience.

"She was playing so well, really making no unforced errors, having a lot of depth and hitting close to the line and I knew it would be difficult to keep on doing what she was doing," said Graf, winner of the last five Grand Slam tournaments she has played.
"I knew it wouldn't be easy today with the conditions out there. It was pretty windy today, but hey, I won so who cares," she said with a smile and a shrug of her shoulders.
The Graf-Hingis match had been suspended by rain after just one game on Friday, but the contest proved worth the wait, filled as it was with long, exciting rallies and tense moments.

Showing a steely calm in the face of adversity that has become a hallmark of Graf's Grand Slam greatness, the German superstar coolly saved five set points in the opening set to frustrate the precocious 16th seed, who was bidding to become the youngest U.S. Open finalist.

Seles and Graf, the co-number one players in the world, have assured a monopoly on the year's major titles. Seles won her fourth Australian Open in January and Graf scooped the French Open and Wimbledon titles.

But Sunday's match will be the first meeting between the great rivals since last year's Open finale, a three-set thriller won by Graf. It will also mark the first repeat of a women's final matchup here since Martina Navratilova and Chris Evert squared off in 1983 and 1984.
Graf preyed on Hingis's inexperience early with some disguised drop shots and tactics designed to leave the 16th seed flat-footed in mid-court.

But it was Hingis, who beat Graf earlier this year in Rome, who came up with the first service break for a 5-3 edge as the German squandered a 40-0 lead on a string of overhit forehands and a backhand error.

The Swiss held her first set point while serving for the set in the next game, but Hingis belted a forehand into the net and threw her racket in disgust. A backhand wide on the next point had the emotional teen bouncing her racket off the court and a missed volley gave Graf the game.
Hingis gave Graf all she could handle in the next game as the German was forced to fend off four more set points before holding for 5-5.
"I had my chances. I'm happy about the way I played," said Hingis, who picked off third seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario and seventh seed Jana Novotna to reach her first Grand Slam semifinal.
"You always want more and more, of course, especially if you have the chance, so I'm a little upset."
A bit rattled by her failure to convert those set points, Hingis dropped the next game and Graf quickly went up 40-0 when serving for the set.
Graf needed only one set point, and perhaps she was picturing the prosecutor who is trying to keep her father behind bars when she unleashed an explosive forehand into the corner to take the set.
On a roll now, Graf broke Hingis to open the second set and held to win her sixth concecutive game.
"I knew there would be a point where she's probably gonna have to make some mistakes and that actually came in the beginning of the second set," Graf said.

But Hingis did not fold, regrouping to keep it close as she saved two break points in the seventh game to pull within 4-3, after which both players left the court to change their sweat-soaked outfits.
Hingis took her time, keeping Graf waiting, and the top seed made her pay for it by winning the next game for 5-3 and building a quick 0-40 lead on Hingis's serve.
Again, the holder of 20 major titles jumped on her first chance to end it, drawing Hingis toward the net before belting a perfect forehand pass down the line for victory.
Afterward, Graf was asked how tough it had been to keep her focus on tennis with her father on trial, facing a 10-year prison sentence on tax evasion charges.
"Pretty difficult," she said.
